title: Rosa and the Bolt
sum: Rosa, her grandpa, her friend Owen and her little brother Tito build a wooden cart called the Bolt, then fix it one problem at a time until race day on Hill Street.

cast.d: a nine-year-old girl who builds and drives the Bolt
cast.look: a nine-year-old girl with a curly black ponytail, a yellow T-shirt, denim shorts and a red bike helmet

cast.d: Rosa's grandpa, a carpenter for forty years who likes a joke
cast.look: a tall older man with a white mustache, a flat gray cap and a carpenter's apron full of pencils

cast.d: Rosa's nine-year-old neighbor and best friend, who measures and times everything
cast.look: a nine-year-old boy with short red hair, freckles, round glasses and a stopwatch on a string around his neck

cast.d: Rosa's five-year-old brother, who makes up loud chants
cast.look: a five-year-old boy with messy black hair, a green dinosaur T-shirt and yellow paint on his hands

cast.d: a ten-year-old racer with a blue cart called the Blue Jay
cast.look: a ten-year-old Japanese American girl with a short black bob, a white helmet and a blue jacket
a woman with gray curls, an orange safety vest and a clipboard

p: The flyer on the library door said HILL STREET DERBY in fat red letters. Underneath were the rules: a wooden cart, no motors, no pedals and one big hill. Rosa copied the date onto the back of her hand: June 14.

Grandpa Luis had been a carpenter for forty years, and his garage smelled like sawdust and coffee. He read the date on Rosa's hand and rubbed his white mustache. “Three weeks is plenty of time,” he said, “if nobody sleeps.” Rosa was already pulling a long board off the shelf.

The board was oak, hard and heavy, and almost as long as Rosa was tall. It would be the floor. Grandpa screwed a thick beam under each end, and Rosa pushed a steel rod through each beam. Four fat rubber wheels from Tito's old red wagon slid onto the ends of the rods.
Tito was five, and he watched it all from an upside-down bucket. “Those are my wagon's wheels,” he said. “You never ride that wagon,” said Rosa. Tito thought about it. “I might ride it tomorrow.”

The front beam had to turn, or the cart could only go straight. Grandpa held up a long silver bolt, as thick as Rosa's thumb. “This holds the front beam on,” he said. “Everything turns around it.” He tightened the nut with a wrench, and Rosa tied a steering rope to each end of the beam.

Last came the brake: a wooden lever by Rosa's right hand, with a rubber pad on the end. When Rosa pulled it, the pad pressed hard on a back wheel. “That's for stopping,” said Grandpa. “Only when you need to.”

“It needs a name,” said Rosa. Grandpa tapped the bolt with his wrench, tink, and Rosa grinned. “The Bolt, like when Noodle hears the vacuum and bolts under the bed!” Noodle was their cat, and she could cross the whole house in two seconds flat.

Tito found a can of yellow paint. Before anyone could stop him, he painted a zigzag down the side of the cart. “It's a lightning bolt,” he said, “so now it means three things.” It also meant Tito had yellow paint up to his elbows.

Grandpa's driveway sloped down to the street, with a mailbox at the bottom. Owen from next door came over with his tape measure, because Owen measured everything. Rosa buckled her red helmet and climbed in, and Grandpa gave the Bolt one tiny push. It rolled forward with a long squeak, eee-eee, and stopped.
“Three meters,” said Owen, reading the tape. “A snail could beat that.” Rosa hopped out and spun a front wheel, but it turned once and stopped with a scrape.
Down on her knees, Rosa saw why. The rubber was rubbing on the wooden beam, and the steel rod was orange with rust. “Rub your hands together, fast,” said Grandpa. Rosa did, and her palms got hot.

“Your wheels are doing that to the wood. Rubbing is good in a brake, but bad in a wheel.” Grandpa opened a jar of shiny washers, flat metal rings like tiny doughnuts. Rosa slid one onto each side of every wheel. Two washers a wheel, four wheels, eight washers.

Then Grandpa put a drop of oil where each wheel met its rod, and Rosa climbed back in. He gave the same tiny push. This time the Bolt did not squeak at all. It rolled past Owen, past the flower pots, all the way to the mailbox.
Owen ran down with the tape and yelled, “Twelve meters!” Tito dipped his brush in the yellow paint again and said, “It needs more lightning now.”

art.s: On a sunny garage driveway, a girl in a red helmet sits in a wooden cart with fat red wagon wheels while her white-mustached grandpa holds an oil can and a small boy paints a yellow lightning bolt on the side.

q.q: Draw one wheel of the Bolt before Grandpa's fix and after it. Show what was rubbing, and what they added.
look: the rubber wheel rubbing on the wooden beam
a washer between the wheel and the wood
a drop of oil on the rod
q.e: Less rubbing means more rolling. You showed the fix!

q.q: The word bolt means more than one thing in this story. Can you write two of its meanings?
q.a: A thick metal pin that holds the front beam on, and running off very fast, like Noodle the cat. (Tito adds a lightning bolt too!)
q.e: One word, three meanings. No wonder Rosa picked it for her cart!

q.q: Before the fix, the Bolt rolled 3 meters. After the fix, it rolled 12 meters. How many times as far is that?
q.e: 3 × 4 = 12, so the Bolt rolled 4 times as far. Those washers worked!

p: On Sunday morning, Grandpa came out of the garage with four skinny black wheels. They came from his old lawn mower, which had not mowed anything in years. The wheels were hard plastic, as tall as the wagon wheels but only half as wide. “Try these,” he said.

Rosa made a face at the skinny wheels. “The fat ones look like monster truck wheels,” she said. “Monster trucks aren't fast,” said Owen. “They're just loud.” Rosa crossed her arms and said, “Fat is faster, and everybody knows it.”

Owen pushed his glasses up his nose. He wore a stopwatch on a string around his neck, and he only took it off for baths. “Then let's test it,” he said. “Three runs on the fat wheels, three on the thin ones.”

The school parking lot had a long, easy slope, and on Sundays it was empty. Grandpa drew a chalk start line at the top and a finish line at the bottom, by the bike rack. Rosa would ride every run, and nobody would push. Each time, Grandpa would hold the back of the Bolt on the start line and just let go.

Tito came along with a paper towel tube and a brand-new chant. He shouted it through the tube before every run: “Go, Bolt, go! Not too slow!” The first time, three pigeons flew off the bike rack at once.

Grandpa let go, and the Bolt rolled down the slope on its fat wheels, bouncing softly over a crack in the blacktop. Click went Owen's stopwatch as the front wheels crossed the line. “Twenty-two seconds,” said Owen. The next two runs were 22 and 23.

Then they swapped the wheels. Pull out the pin, slide off the wheel, slide on the new one, put the pin back. The washers and the oil went back on too. Tito tried to count every second out loud, but he gave up at 97.

The first run on the thin wheels felt different right away. The Bolt rattled a little over the crack, but the wheels made a fast, low hum on the blacktop. “Eighteen seconds!” Owen shouted, and he almost dropped his pencil. The next two runs were 19 and 18.

Owen turned his notebook around to show a table with two columns, FAT and THIN, and three times in each. Rosa pressed her thumb into a fat wagon wheel, and it squished like a marshmallow. The thin wheel did not squish at all.

“But the fat ones felt smoother,” said Rosa. “Smooth isn't fast,” said Grandpa. “A soft wheel squashes flat at the bottom as it rolls, and that slows it down. It's like riding your bike on a flat tire.” Rosa had done that once, all the way home from school, and her legs still remembered it.
Rosa stared at the table for a long time. “Okay, I was wrong,” she said at last. “Thin is faster.” Owen did not say “I told you so.” He just drew a small star at the top of the THIN column.
Back home, Tito climbed into the red wagon before its last fat wheel was even on. Rosa pulled him around the yard three times, and he chanted the whole way. “Go, wagon, go! Not too slow!”

art.s: In an empty school parking lot on a gentle slope, a girl in a red helmet rolls a wooden cart with thin black wheels past a chalk finish line while a boy with glasses clicks a stopwatch and a little boy shouts through a paper towel tube.

q.q: Turn Owen's table into a bar graph. Draw one bar for the first fat-wheel run and one for the first thin-wheel run.
look: a bar for 22 seconds and a bar for 18 seconds
q.e: A shorter bar means fewer seconds, and fewer seconds means faster. 22 − 18 = 4 seconds!

q.q: Rosa rode every run, and nobody pushed. Why did they keep those things the same?
c: So only the wheels would change
So the Bolt would go faster
So Rosa would not get tired
q.e: When only one thing changes, you know that thing made the difference.

q.q: Owen and Tito both came to help. How was Owen's job different from Tito's?
q.a: Owen timed each run with his stopwatch and wrote the times in a table. Tito shouted chants through a tube.
q.e: Owen helped with numbers, and Tito helped with noise. A team needs both!

p: The next Saturday was sign-up day at the fire station. Racers waited with their carts in the big garage, right beside the red fire truck. Rosa pulled the Bolt by its ropes, and the thin wheels hummed on the smooth floor. A firefighter saw the yellow lightning bolts and gave her a thumbs-up.

In line ahead of them stood a girl in a white helmet, next to a shiny blue cart. Its nose came to a point like a bird's beak, and BLUE JAY was painted on the side. The girl looked at the Bolt's lightning bolts and grinned. “I'm Hana,” she said. “Fast name.”

The judge, Mrs. Greene, wore an orange vest and handed out sign-up cards. The last line on the card said: “Why do you want to race?” Rosa chewed her pencil, then wrote, “Grandpa and I built it. I want to see how fast it goes.”

A sign hung above the scale: CART + DRIVER = 70 KG OR LESS. First Rosa stood on the flat metal scale in her helmet, and it said 32 kg. Then Grandpa and Owen lifted the Bolt onto the scale, and it said 41 kg.
Owen wrote both numbers in his notebook and started to add, but halfway through, his pencil stopped. He looked at the sign, then back at his notebook, and said, “Uh-oh.”
“Too heavy,” said Mrs. Greene. “Fix it, and come back on Wednesday to weigh again.” Rosa's ears went hot, and she stared at the floor.
Hana leaned over and whispered, “Mine was too heavy last year, so I took off my cup holder.” The Bolt did not even have a cup holder.
At home, everyone had an idea. “Rosa can skip lunch!” said Tito. Grandpa shook his head and said, “Nobody skips lunch in my house.”
Tito tried again. “Take off one wheel?” Owen drew a three-wheeled cart in his notebook, lying on its side, with a tiny helmet rolling away. Tito went to find a snack instead.

Grandpa knocked on the Bolt's floor, knock, knock. It sounded solid, like a front door. “It's oak,” he said, “strong as a bull and heavy as one.” He dug through his woodpile and pulled out a pale yellow pine board.

Rosa wanted to see for herself. In the scrap box she found two small blocks, one oak and one pine, exactly the same size. She laid a ruler across a round pencil, like a tiny seesaw, and set a block on each end. With a clack, the oak end dropped to the table, and the pine end tipped up.
“Same size, different weight,” said Owen. Grandpa held the pine block up to the window. “Pine has more tiny air spaces inside, like a sponge cake next to a brownie,” he said.

Tito yelled from the kitchen, “Are there brownies?” There were no brownies, but there was a new floor to make. Grandpa sawed the pine to size, and Rosa sanded it until her arms ached. Before they screwed it on, she put each board on the bathroom scale. The old oak board was 9 kg, and the new pine board was 5 kg.

On Wednesday, Rosa sat in the Bolt, and Grandpa rolled them both onto the big scale. “Sixty-nine,” said Mrs. Greene, and she stamped Rosa's card with a green stamp: PASSED. Tito held out the back of his hand, so she stamped that too.

art.s: Inside a fire station garage beside a red fire truck, a judge in an orange vest reads a flat metal scale while a white-mustached grandpa and a boy with glasses lift a wooden cart with yellow lightning bolts onto it.

q.q: Rosa weighed 32 kg and the Bolt weighed 41 kg. The sign said 70 kg or less. How much too heavy were they?
q.e: Together they weighed 73 kg. That's 3 kg too much, about as heavy as three one-liter bottles of water.

q.q: What is this part of the story mostly about?
c: Making the Bolt light enough to race
Painting lightning bolts on the Bolt
Timing the Bolt in the parking lot
Helping Hana take off her cup holder
q.e: The scale, the seesaw and the pine board all help with one job: getting the weight down.

q.q: Draw Rosa's ruler seesaw with the oak block and the pine block on it. Show which end went down.
look: a ruler lying across a round pencil
the oak end down and the pine end up
q.e: Same size, different weight. Your seesaw shows it!

p: On Friday evening, the night before the race, Hill Street was closed to cars for practice. The course ran 200 meters, from a wooden start ramp at the top to a finish line by the library. Three orange flags split it into four equal parts. At the top, a metal gate held each cart on the ramp until the judge dropped it.

Rosa's turn was near the end, so she spent 40 minutes checking every pin and every washer. Then she checked them again. Hana went just before her, and the Blue Jay shot down the hill without a single wobble. Down at the finish, Owen clicked his stopwatch: 28 seconds. He timed everybody, whether they asked or not.

From the top, Hill Street looked twice as steep as it did from the bottom. Rosa pulled her helmet strap tight and grabbed the ropes. Her stomach felt like a jar of jumping beans. With a clank, the gate dropped, and the Bolt rolled off the ramp.

Wind roared in Rosa's ears as the Bolt picked up speed, faster than it had ever gone before. In the first part of the hill, her hand grabbed the brake lever all by itself. Screech went the rubber pad against the back wheel. She let go, sped up, and grabbed the brake again in the third part.
At the finish line, Owen looked at his stopwatch. “Thirty-four seconds,” he said. In his notebook, he drew the hill in four parts and marked each brake spot with a small red X.
“It was so fast,” Rosa said, and her cheeks burned. Grandpa patted the Bolt's nose. “That's the whole idea,” he said.

Tito had been chanting at the finish line the whole time, but Rosa had not heard one word. The wind was blowing down the hill, parents were chattering, and the top was far away. Tito's shoulders sagged. “I was so loud,” he said.

Owen got a sheet of poster board from Grandpa's truck, rolled it into a big cone and taped the side. “Talk into the small end,” he told Tito. “Your voice spreads out everywhere, like ripples in a pond. The cone sends more of it one way.”

Tito pointed the cone up the hill and shouted, “BOLT!” Far up the street, a man in a cap turned around to look. Rosa laughed for the first time all evening. Then Tito sat down on the curb, counting beats on his fingers and whispering words.
When he jumped up, he had a new chant. “Bolt, Bolt, from the top! Hold the ropes and never stop!” Owen wrote it down, and Tito made him read it back twice.

The sun was low when Rosa's second turn came. Tito stood by the middle flag, halfway down, with the paper cone pointed up the hill. The gate dropped with a clank, and in the first part, Rosa's hand twitched toward the brake. Then she heard it, loud and clear: “Never stop!”

She held the ropes with both hands and let the Bolt go, and the flags flew past, one, two, three. Down by the library, Owen yelled, “Twenty-nine seconds!” Tito came running down the sidewalk with the paper cone on his head, like a party hat.

art.s: At sunset on a steep street marked with three orange flags, a little boy shouts up the hill through a big paper cone as a wooden cart with yellow lightning bolts rolls down from a wooden start ramp.

q.q: Why do you think Tito put “never stop” in his new chant?
c: The judge said to keep going.
q.e: Rosa braked two times on her first run. Tito's chant told her to keep going.

q.q: Why could Rosa hear Tito better when he used the paper cone?
q.a: The cone sent more of his voice one way, up the hill toward Rosa, instead of letting it spread out everywhere.
q.e: Cupping your hands around your mouth works the same way!

q.q: Draw Hill Street from ramp to finish in 4 equal parts. Color the parts where Rosa braked on her first run. What fraction did you color?
look: the hill split into 4 equal parts
2 parts colored: the first and the third
q.e: She braked in 2 of the 4 parts. 2/4 is half the hill!

p: On Saturday morning, Hill Street was lined with lawn chairs. Kids sat on the curbs with juice boxes, and a man on the corner sold lemonade for a dollar. Eight racers waited at the top with their carts. Tito had painted a lightning bolt on his paper cone, and one on his cheek.

All morning, carts clanked off the ramp two at a time and rattled down the hill. In Rosa's first race, she beat a boy whose cart was shaped like a hot dog, mustard and all. Then she beat a girl in a purple cart, just barely. By eleven o'clock, two racers were left for the final: Hana in the Blue Jay and Rosa in the Bolt.

The final was two runs, one in each lane. Mrs. Greene would add up each racer's two times, and the smaller total would win. For the first run, Rosa had Lane 2 and Hana had Lane 1. The gates dropped together with one big clank.
Rosa held the ropes and did not touch the brake once. But she sat up tall to look for Hana, and the wind pushed on her chest like a big hand. The Blue Jay crossed the line first.
The judge wrote the times on a chalkboard by the finish line: Hana 27 seconds, Rosa 28 seconds. Rosa's shoulders dropped. She was one second behind, just long enough to say “one Mississippi.”

While volunteers towed the carts back up the hill, Owen jogged beside the Bolt. “Remember riding your bike home against the wind? You ducked down low, and it got easier.” Rosa remembered. Her nose had almost touched the handlebars.
“So duck down, chin low and back flat,” said Owen. “Less air will push on you. I bet you'll go faster.” He pushed up his glasses. “Probably.”
At the top, Grandpa checked every pin one last time. Hana leaned out of the Blue Jay and said, “Good luck.” Rosa wiped her sweaty hands on her shorts and took the ropes.

For the second run, the racers switched lanes. Rosa tucked her chin down until she could just see over the front of the Bolt. The gates clanked, and this time the wind slid over her helmet instead of her chest. Halfway down, a voice came through a paper cone: “BOLT, BOLT, FROM THE TOP!”
This time Rosa kept her eyes on the finish line and never once looked for Hana. The Bolt crossed first, but nobody cheered yet. Everyone turned to look at the judge.

Mrs. Greene wrote the new times on the chalkboard: Rosa 25 seconds, Hana 27 seconds. Her chalk squeaked as she added up each girl's two times, and the whole street waited. “The winner,” she said, “is Rosa and the Bolt!”
Tito screamed so loud that he did not need the cone. Hana climbed out of the Blue Jay and walked straight over, grinning. “You ducked,” she said. “Next year, I'm ducking too.”
The two girls bumped helmets, clonk, instead of shaking hands. Mrs. Greene gave Rosa a blue ribbon, and Grandpa tied it to the Bolt's steering rope.

On the way home, Grandpa pulled the Bolt up the sidewalk with Tito inside, fast asleep. The paper cone was still in his lap. “Next year,” Grandpa said, “we build two.” Owen was already writing it down.

art.s: At the bottom of a crowded street with lawn chairs, a girl ducked low in a wooden cart with yellow lightning bolts crosses the finish line ahead of a blue cart, while a judge in an orange vest stands by a chalkboard of times.

q.q: Draw Rosa and Hana right after the race. Give Hana a speech bubble. What did she say that shows she is a good sport?
look: Rosa and Hana together near their carts
a speech bubble with Hana's kind words, like “You ducked. Next year, I'm ducking too.”
q.e: Hana lost by just one second and still came over grinning. That's a good sport!

q.q: Add up each girl's two times. By how many seconds did Rosa win?
q.a: By 1 second. Rosa had 28 + 25 = 53 seconds, and Hana had 27 + 27 = 54 seconds.
q.e: 53 is just one less than 54. That's one Mississippi!

q.q: Owen predicted that ducking down would make Rosa faster. What was his reason?
c: Less air would push on her.
She could see the finish better.
q.e: Sitting up tall is like holding up a sail. Ducking low lets the air slide over you.

fin.q: The Bolt got faster and faster in this story. Name two changes that helped.
fin.a: Washers and oil on the wheels, and the thin mower wheels. Not braking and ducking low helped too.
fin.e: Every change took away a little rubbing, squishing or pushing air.

fin.q: Rosa's first practice run down Hill Street took 34 seconds. How much faster was her second run in the final?
fin.e: Her second run in the final took 25 seconds. 34 − 25 = 9 seconds faster!
